studies.title: Scene-based field validation of wearable light loggers
studies.reference: JETI Spectraval 1501 in Tübingen; Konica Minolta CL-500A in Izmir.
studies.protocol: Fixed tripod rig sampled 433 indoor/outdoor scenes across daylight, artificial and mixed lighting in Tübingen and Izmir. Bootstrap resampling assessed sampling requirements.
studies.finding: Across 433 scenes, both devices tracked the spectral reference measurements closely but systematically underestimated light levels.
studies.limitations: Preprint. Tripod measurements do not establish continuous on-body accuracy. Only one ActTrust2 unit and two ActLumus units were tested, with one ActLumus at each site.
studies.notes: arXiv v1, 16 June 2026. Both devices measured photopic illuminance; only ActLumus measured melanopic EDI. The same ActTrust2 unit was used at both sites.

studies.title: Evaluation of wearable light dosimeters for circadian lighting: spectral, spatial, photometric, melanopic, and thermal performance
studies.reference: Calibrated Gigahertz-Optik BTS256 spectroradiometer; cosine-law angular benchmark.
studies.protocol: Three units per model tested under controlled LEDs (0–570 lx) and partly cloudy daylight (42,000–78,000 lx), with separate angular and temperature tests.
studies.finding: Speck had the closest photopic agreement of the three models overall; all three showed poorer performance under high daylight levels. Melanopic EDI was tested for Speck and LYS Button under LED lighting. Agreement was poorer for LYS at low light levels. Angle tests used photopic illuminance, with Speck closest to the cosine reference.
studies.limitations: Three units per type; one short daylight session; spectral reconstruction evaluated for only one Speck; no on-body position or occlusion testing. Daylight variability limits interpretation as a strict linearity test.
studies.notes: Published 21 July 2026. Results concern Speck v1.0, not v2.0. Melanopic EDI was evaluated only for LYS Button and Speck under LEDs; Actiwatch was excluded because it lacks melanopic outputs. Spectral reconstruction testing applies only to Speck.

studies.title: Performance of wearable light sensors for measuring photopic and melanopic illuminance under laboratory and free-living conditions
studies.reference: NIST-calibrated ILT560-A spectrometer; free-living comparison between ActLumus and ActiGraph.
studies.protocol: Eight units per manufacturer tested under warm/cool LEDs (2–1,000 lx) and daylight (5,000–100,000 lx). Twenty-one adults wore ActLumus and ActiGraph concurrently for one week.
studies.finding: Average photopic errors across the tested intensities were 3.3% for ActLumus, 19.5% for LYS, −35.7% for GENEActiv and −68.0% for ActiGraph wGT3X-BT. The study separately examined detection thresholds, linearity and saturation.
studies.limitations: Two indoor spectra and selected daylight conditions do not cover all lighting environments. The field component compared two wrist devices without a continuously worn reference spectrometer.
studies.notes: Online November 2025; February 2026 issue. Melanopic testing applies only to ActLumus and LYS. The paper uses melanopic illuminance/lux, not explicitly EDI; indexed here as Other circadian metrics. LYS hardware version is unspecified. Between-unit variability is distinct from repeatability. Additional reported endpoints: Dynamic range, Between-device variability. The LYS name is indexed under LYS Button; these are the same device, as clarified by the curator. The paper does not specify a hardware revision.

studies.title: Validation of real-time viewing distance and ambient illumination measurement with two wearable sensors
studies.reference: Calibrated Konica Minolta CL-200A chroma meter for illumination; ruler for the separate distance assessment.
studies.protocol: Five units of each model attached to spectacles on a mannequin. Light measurements were repeated across seven indoor/outdoor locations on three days. A separate study tested viewing distance in 13 young adults.
studies.finding: Both devices tracked the calibrated lux meter. Differences became more variable above about 3500 lux for Clouclip and 4000 lux for Vivior.
studies.limitations: The participant component assessed viewing distance rather than light-measurement accuracy during unrestricted wear. The study did not validate melanopic or spectral outputs; sleep mode and spectacle use can affect deployment.
studies.notes: Published 14 February 2025. Exact tested versions were five Vivior Mark 3+ and five second-generation Clouclip units. Agreement in photopic illuminance should not be generalized to other outputs or hardware generations. Outdoor-threshold discussion is not indexed as classification validation.

studies.title: Beyond Lux: methods for species and photoreceptor-specific quantification of ambient light for mammals
studies.reference: Calibrated SpectroCal spectroradiometer; species-specific photoreceptor weighting functions.
studies.protocol: Ten-channel readings were fitted to reference measurements from 13 spectra, then tested at a wider range of irradiances. Performance was assessed for 12 domestic mammal species and humans.
studies.finding: Melanopic and rhodopic estimates performed better than short-wavelength cone estimates; limited UV sensitivity constrained some species-specific quantities.
studies.limitations: Bench calibration of wearable hardware, not an on-body validation. Accuracy depends on the spectra and species-specific response being estimated.

studies.title: Wearable light spectral sensor optimized for measuring daily α-opic light exposure
studies.reference: Konica Minolta CL-500A calibrated illuminance spectrophotometer.
studies.protocol: A pendant/clip spectrophotometer covering 380–780 nm was developed and tested with common light sources; corrections addressed directionality, dark noise, saturation, nonlinearity, stray light and spectral response.
studies.finding: For four tested source types, α-opic EDI errors were below 7% after calibration. Adding a diffuser brought the sensor’s angular response closer to a cosine curve.
studies.limitations: Bench testing of a prototype with four source types does not establish accuracy for every spectrum or wearing condition. No equivalence to a later branded device is inferred.

studies.title: Accuracy of the GENEActiv Device for Measuring Light Exposure in Sleep and Circadian Research
studies.reference: J17 Luma Color illuminance meter; MK350N spectrometer for spectral measurements.
studies.protocol: Ten units tested under fluorescent and LED illumination, darkness, overcast outdoor daylight, narrowband blue/green/red LEDs and an infrared camera illuminator.
studies.finding: Outputs tracked illuminance but generally underestimated it, particularly below 100 lux. Accuracy depended on spectrum: green light was under-reported, red light over-reported, and infrared affected the measurements.
studies.limitations: Low-light accuracy varied by source. Recording relative light patterns or distinguishing indoor/outdoor conditions does not establish accurate absolute exposure in dim environments.
studies.notes: Clocks & Sleep 2(2), 143–152. Inter-device reliability is reported separately from repeatability; findings apply to tested hardware/software. Additional reported endpoints: Low-light response, Inter-device reliability.

studies.title: Determining Light Intensity, Timing and Type of Visible and Circadian Light From an Ambulatory Circadian Monitoring Device
studies.reference: Ocean Optics spectroradiometer with CC-3 cosine corrector; CIE S 026 calculations from reference spectra.
studies.protocol: Commercial lamps and sunlight were compared with three-channel Kronowise readings; separate calibration relationships were developed for natural and two artificial-light classes.
studies.finding: Source-dependent infrared correction improved agreement between Kronowise and the reference spectroradiometer; the corrected photopic regression had a slope of 0.994 and correlation of 0.997.
studies.limitations: Results depend on the source classifier and fitted calibration. The paper’s circadian channel is not automatically interchangeable with every modern melanopic EDI implementation.

studies.reference: Lux meter and UV sensor; models unresolved in the inspected abstract.

studies.limitations: Abstract-level calibration record. The observational refractive-error comparisons do not themselves validate the sensor; quantitative accuracy requires full-text extraction.

studies.title: Optical performance characterization of light-logging actigraphy dosimeters
studies.reference: Photopic and photoreceptor sensitivity functions, cosine response and reference values for dynamic characterization.
studies.protocol: New optical tests and existing evidence were combined. This record indexes four complete-protocol models with individually identifiable spectral and angular results: MotionWatch 8, ActTrust, GENEActiv Original and Actiwatch 2.
studies.finding: Optical characterization covers directional and spectral sensitivity, linearity, dynamic range and resolution, with a proposed assessment protocol. Results are model- and channel-specific.
studies.limitations: Only abstract and publisher tables were inspected. Other models discussed in the paper are omitted here to avoid counting reused evidence or assigning combined model results to individual variants.
studies.notes: Abstract and Tables 1–4 inspected. Indexed coverage restricted to individually identifiable spectral and angular tests. Additional reported endpoints: Linearity, Dynamic range, Resolution.

studies.title: Comparison and Correction of the Light Sensor Output from 48 Wearable Light Exposure Devices by Using a Side-by-Side Field Calibration Method
studies.reference: Forty-eight Actiwatch Spectrum units measured side by side; white-channel response also compared with a calibrated photometer.
studies.protocol: RGB and white outputs were compared under different light sources to develop a field-calibration procedure.
studies.finding: Light responses differed by up to 60% between units. The authors proposed side-by-side field calibration to reduce these differences.
studies.limitations: Agreement after field correction does not by itself establish traceable absolute accuracy. Detailed correction coefficients require the full paper.

studies.title: Comparisons of three practical field devices used to measure personal light exposures and activity levels
studies.reference: Photopic V(λ), cosine response and calibrated near-eye Daysimeter measurements for placement comparisons.
studies.protocol: Optical characterization and field comparisons: 12 adults over 65 wore Daysimeters at four body locations and a wrist Actiwatch; five days analyzed.
studies.finding: Six Daysimeter-D units and six Actiwatch Spectrum units were compared with a calibrated photometer under five light sources; Daysimeter-D showed closer photopic agreement.
studies.limitations: Neither device qualified as a laboratory-grade photometer. Field evidence is from older adults; circadian light and stimulus are model-specific quantities, not CIE melanopic EDI.
studies.notes: Five of seven days analyzed. Placement comparisons used Daysimeters; Actiwatch remained at the wrist.

studies.title: The Daysimeter: a device for measuring optical radiation as a stimulus for the human circadian system
studies.reference: Photo Research LRS 450 Light Standard; spectral matching against the photopic response.
studies.protocol: Two prototypes were checked for spectral response. Linearity was tested against an integrating-sphere source with an approximately illuminant-A spectrum.
studies.finding: Photopic spectral-mismatch values were 3.8% and 5.4%. The tested response departed from linearity by a few percent across roughly 3.5 decades of irradiance.
studies.limitations: Partial full-text extraction from the indexed author PDF. The instrument’s higher advertised range was not tested. This record does not establish modern melanopic EDI accuracy.
